newsitem.title: FALKLAND ISLANDS: Argentine next-of-kin visit sparks Falklands ire.
newsitem.headline: Argentine next-of-kin visit sparks Falklands ire.

text.p: Families of Argentine servicemen buried on the Falklands will visit war graves on Wednesday in the teeth of bitter opposition from the fiercely pro-British islanders.
Although relatives have visited the Argentine war cemetery near Darwin before, the Falklanders remain deeply mistrustful of a country that still lays claim to the islands it calls the Malvinas.
British authorities have urged the Falklanders to take a more conciliatory approach to such visits, 15 years after a British task force drove an Argentine invasion force from the islands.

A group of 15 Argentines, accompanied by a priest, will arrive on the Falklands on Wednesday. They will hold a graveside service out of view of residents of Darwin and neighbouring Goose Green, scene of some of the 1982 war's worst fighting.
Another group of 15 will visit the cemetery in February. Previous visits to Argentine war dead took place in 1995, 1991 and 1986.

The cemetery contains the graves of 234 Argentine servicemen, many identified only as "Conscripto" (Conscript) or "Soldado" (Soldier). On 123 crosses are written the words "An Argentine soldier known unto God".
The rest of the Argentine war dead were lost at sea. The known death toll for the six-week war was 652 Argentines and 255 Britons.
Falklands councillors wanted a larger, one-off visit by the Argentine relatives. They were also opposed to the families staying overnight and being lodged at Darwin.
"We have had to concede on all three of our demands," said councillor Norma Edwards.
The families will be flown in on a U.S.-registered aircraft from Buenos Aires. During their stay they will be "discreetly" supervised by civilian police, officials said.
Falklands residents, who fear they will eventually have to accept monthly visits from Argentine families, have called for the Argentines to take the bodies of their war dead back to the mainland.
But hardliners in Buenos Aires have refused, saying the bodies are buried on Argentine soil in the Malvinas.
